messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kiet Pham is a forty-year-old Vietnamese-American journalist, currently divorced and living alone in a one-bedroom apartment in Houston. He came to the clinic after his editor placed him on indefinite leave, citing erratic behaviour and missed deadlines — a professional collapse that, in his own words, "finally made it impossible to pretend I was functioning."

Approximately fourteen months ago, Kiet was detained while reporting on labour conditions in a Southeast Asian country he had visited on assignment. Over the course of several days he was subjected to systematic physical and psychological torture by state security personnel. He was kept in a windowless room, deprived of sleep, beaten repeatedly, and at one point restrained while the muffled cries of children — detainees in an adjacent cell — filtered through the concrete wall. His captors used his full name with deliberate, almost ceremonial precision each time they addressed him before inflicting pain, so that the syllables of his own name became inseparable from what followed. There were periods he cannot account for at all: stretches of time that exist in his memory only as absence, bordered by images so extreme — the texture of a drain cover against his cheek, a guard's boot — that he has sometimes struggled to believe they happened to him rather than to someone he once interviewed.

When Kiet returned to the United States, the symptoms began quietly and then gathered force. The most immediate and destabilising triggers were sounds: a child crying in a supermarket aisle, the dizzy, nauseating lurch that arrived without warning in his inner ear, or hearing his own name — or names phonetically close to it — spoken aloud in an ordinary conversation. Each of these sensations pulled him back toward the memory with a violence that felt physical, and as they did, the fragmentary, gap-ridden quality of what he could recall made the intrusions worse rather than better. He could not deliberately reconstruct the sequence of events in any coherent way — the memory resisted orderly retrieval — and this incompleteness meant that when a trigger struck, what surfaced was not narrative but sensation: raw, contextless, and without edges. The gaps in his memory, rather than offering relief, left him in a state of chronic unresolved arousal, as though the story could not be filed because it had no ending he could access.

His appraisals of himself darkened steadily across the months following his return. He had come to believe, with a certainty he found difficult to articulate but impossible to dismiss, that something was fundamentally broken in him — not wounded, but defective, as though the events had revealed a flaw that had always been there. He was certain that people on the street could see it simply by looking at him, that his face or his bearing broadcast what had been done to him and, worse, what he believed he had allowed. He had acted in ways during his captivity that violated his own sense of who he was — he could not be more specific than that in session, and the memory gaps made precision impossible — and the shame this produced was not situational but ontological. These appraisals fed directly back into his sensitivity to triggers: hearing his name spoken casually by a colleague felt unbearable precisely because he believed the name now carried the mark of what he was. The shame also intensified his hypervigilance; convinced that others could read his degradation, he watched people's faces and body language with exhausting attention, scanning for signs of contempt or threat, which in turn kept his nervous system in a state of perpetual alarm and made ordinary sounds — a door slamming, a laugh in the corridor — land like blows.

The strategies Kiet developed to manage this state became, over time, their own form of damage. He stopped seeing the colleagues and friends he had known before the assignment, telling himself he could not bear for them to witness whatever they would inevitably see in him. He began eating less and less, not from appetite loss alone but as a form of control — one of the few domains in which he felt any agency — and the physical depletion this produced worsened his dizziness, which was itself a trigger, creating a loop he recognised intellectually but could not interrupt. He spent long hours at his desk not writing but replaying the lead-up to his detention, dwelling on every decision point, every moment at which he might have left earlier or filed differently or said something different to his fixer. This rumination, which felt like problem-solving, kept the traumatic material active and close, so that the threshold for the next intrusion lowered further. His withdrawal from social contact meant there was no one to interrupt the cycle, no relational friction to pull him back into ordinary time. His editor's call came after he submitted a piece that made no coherent sense — he had not noticed.

What Kiet most fears, sitting in the waiting room of this clinic, is that the defectiveness he feels is the accurate account of himself, and that therapy will confirm rather than challenge it. What he most hopes, though he has not yet said this aloud, is that someone will help him find the parts of the story he cannot remember — not because he wants to relive them, but because he has come to believe, quietly and desperately, that he cannot be a whole person until the gaps are filled.
